primary_claim: A Claude-based prompt evaluator can block up to 100% of ProtocolQA bioweapon-adjacent prompts when the evaluator task is carefully worded ('weapon-related sciences evaluation'), but a nearly synonymous phrasing that includes the word 'weapons' blocks far fewer prompts (12.5% or 64%), showing that blocking effectiveness is highly sensitive to instruction wording.

effect.metric: percentage of ProtocolQA prompts blocked by the prompt evaluator
effect.value: Anti-jailbreak task: <8%; Safety evaluation task: ~33%; Weapon evaluation 1: 12.5%; Weapon evaluation 2: 64%; Weapon-related sciences evaluation: 100%

contradicts_or_qualifies: Luca Righetti (Open Philanthropy) argued that OpenAI's o1 CBRN test conclusions are unclear and that the model may be more dangerous than OpenAI's system card indicates
stated_future_work: Research into more active prompt evaluator task generation, e.g. mimicking Best-of-N jailbreaking techniques to algorithmically search over evaluator instruction wording to maximize prompt-blocking performance on a given benchmark
limitations_stated: Large differences in blocking effectiveness result from subtle, seemingly synonymous changes in evaluator task wording, demonstrating instability in the approach
quote: That got the desired 100% blockage ('Weapon-related sciences evaluation.')
